issues.title: Invalid DE sampled-sum and convergence-factor bound
issues.failure_explanation: From eq:DE and eq:Pjs, for N=1, h=2, i=1 and j=0 one has |e_{1,0}|=(b-a)(π/4+Si(π)/2). Since Si(π)>1, this is greater than (b-a)(π/4+1/2)>1.1(b-a). Hence a single term contradicts eq:Ebound. The preceding proof merely writes the sampled sum as approximately equal to an integral and supplies no valid upper inequality.
issues.overall_effect: The bound on E, the resulting rational estimate for the inverse, and consequently the convergence-factor bound in Th3-2 are not established. Th3-1, which is conditional on the actual value of the matrix norm, is unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the approximate sum-to-integral step by a rigorous sampled-sum estimate. For g(s)=(π/2)cosh(s)/cosh²((π/2)sinh(s)), prove that g is even and decreasing on [0,∞), so that h∑_{j∈ℤ}g(jh)≤2+(π/2)h. This yields ‖E‖∞≤1.1(b−a)(1+πh/4). Then replace the hypothesis of Th3-2 by q:=1.1L(b−a)(1+πh/4)<1 and replace its denominator by 1−q. The resulting theorem retains the same method, dimension independence, and O((log N)²/N) bound when h=O(log N/N).
issues.why_classification: The false sampled-sum inequality is not a transcription error and cannot be repaired by merely changing an approximation sign. A complete repair requires a new discrete-sum lemma and corresponding changes to the theorem's hypothesis and convergence-factor formula, exceeding a routine local correction. Nevertheless, this work is confined to the norm-estimation subsection, and the modest small-h restriction leaves a recognizably comparable Th3-2 with the same asymptotic rate and convergence guarantee. Thus a contained, limited-loss resolution exists.

issues.title: Nonlinear Example 3 lies outside the advertised theorem regime

failure_location.quote: In this section, we present some numerical examples that confirm the validity of Theorems \ref{Th3-1} and \ref{Th3-2}.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We also investigate the actual value of $\|M_{\rm GS}\|_{\infty}$ as a function of $N$ and compare it with the bound \eqref{eq:MGSNorm2}.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose presents the numerical examples as confirming both Th3-1 and Th3-2. In old Example 3, b-a=1 and ρ=1/2. On the stated box, f1=x1x2 forces every Lipschitz constant to satisfy L≥7/2, while every uniform bound satisfies M≥5/2. Thus 1.1L(b-a)≥3.85, violating the explicit hypothesis of Th3-2, and Assumption 3-1(iii) requires w≤ρ/M≤1/5. For h=log N/N and N≥2, the last row of the DE weight matrix instead gives w>(b-a)/5. The old source therefore supplies numerical behavior outside the theorem regime, not theorem-based validation of its nonlinear experiment; that distinction is material because Example 3 is the only nonlinear example.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical evidence overstates the demonstrated nonlinear applicability of the convergence analysis. The formal statements of Th3-1 and Th3-2 are not themselves invalidated by this independent example-regime defect.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Revise the section opening and the discussion and captions for old Example 3 to state that only examples satisfying Assumption 3-1 and the hypotheses of Th3-2 provide theorem-based confirmation. Explicitly identify the [0,1] Lotka–Volterra experiment as an empirical illustration outside that regime, and do not present its behavior or the displayed formula as a validated theorem bound.
issues.why_classification: This is a substantive evidentiary overclaim, not a wording typo. The qualification is local and leaves the formal theorems and in-regime examples unchanged, but it necessarily withdraws the paper's only claimed nonlinear validation, so it entails meaningful yet limited loss and cannot be minor. A recognizably comparable numerical-evidence claim survives without any reconstruction of the theory, so the issue is not serious.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Hence, we can set the integration interval $[a,b]$ to $[0,\rho/M]=[0,\frac{2}{9}]$. Then, $(b-a)L=\frac{11}{9}$ and we have $\|M_{\rm GS}\|_{\infty}<1$ for $N\ge 16$.
